But because these things are trivial, and are not conducive to piety, I only slightly touch upon them; and would even omit them entirely, except that, to remove a scruple from the minds of the unskillful, is sometimes useful, if it be but done sparingly and with brevity.<div eID="gen5411" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.43.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5410" osisID="Gen.43.25" type="section"/>
entries.3d489329ea726af6e3f3488c447542709bfdfce8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.43.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.43.32" sID="gen5412" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32. </hi><hi type="italic">Because the Egyptians might not eat, etc</hi> <note n="169"> <div sID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> “At the entertainment to which Joseph invited his brethren, they sat apart from the Egyptians, while Joseph was again separated from both. The author [Moses} shows the reason of this in the remark, ‘Because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.’ <hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi> also remarks, that the Egyptians abstained from all familiar intercourse with foreigners, since these were unclean to them, especially because they slew and ate the animals which were sacred among the Egyptians. The circumstance that Joseph eats separately from the other Egyptians is strictly in accordance with the great difference of rank, and the spirit of caste, which prevailed among the Egyptians.” — Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 39. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> </note> Moses says they might not eat with the Hebrews, because they abhorred it, as being unlawful. For seeing that their religion forbade it, they were so bound, that they could not do what they did not dare to do. This passage teaches us how great was the pride of that nation; for, whence did it arise that they so utterly detested the Hebrews, unless because they thought themselves alone to be pure and holy in the world, and acceptable to God? God, indeed, commands his worshipers to abstain from all the pollutions of the Gentiles. But it behaves any one who separates himself from others, to be himself pure and upright. Therefore superstitious persons vainly attempt to claim this privilege for themselves, seeing they carry their impurity within, and are destitute of sincerity. Superstition, also, is affected with another disease; namely, that it is full of pride, so that it despises all men, under the pretext that they are vicious. It is asked, however, whether the Egyptians were separated from Joseph, because they regarded him as polluted: for this the words of Moses seem to intimate. If this interpretation is received, then they esteemed their false religion so highly, that they did not scruple to load their governor with reproaches. I rather conjecture, that Joseph sat apart from them, for the sake of honor; since it would be absurd that they, who disdained to sit at the same table with him, should be invited as his guests. Therefore it is probable that this distinct order was made by Joseph himself, that he might maintain his own dignity; and yet that the sons of Jacob were not mixed with the Egyptians, because the former were an abomination to the latter. For though the origin of Joseph was known, yet he had so passed over to the Egyptians, that he had become as one of their body. For which reason, also, the king had given him a name, when he adorned him with the insignia of his office as chief governor. Now, when we see that the church of God was, at that time, so proudly despised by profane men, we need not wonder that we also, at the present day, are subjected to similar reproach. Meanwhile, we must endeavor to keep ourselves pure from the filth of the world, for the Lord’s sake; and yet this desire must be so at tempered, that we may be alienated from the vices, rather than from the persons of men. For on this account does God sanctify his children, that they may beware of the vices of the unbelievers among whom they are conversant; and nevertheless may allure, as many as are curable, to a participation of their piety. Two things are here to be attended to; first, that we may be fully persuaded of the genuineness of our faith; secondly, that our excessive and fruitless fastidiousness may not entirely alienate many from the Lord, who otherwise might have been won. For we are not expressly commanded so to abhor the wicked, as not eat with them; but to avoid such association as may subject us to the same yoke. Besides, this passage confirms what I have before said, that the Hebrews had derived their name, not from their passing over the river; (as some falsely imagine,) but from their ancestor Heber. Nor was the fame of a single small and distantly situated family, sufficiently celebrated in Egypt, to become the cause of public dissension.<div eID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.43.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5412" osisID="Gen.43.32" type="section"/>
entries.6f81cb1f2ee1c95e886cef2782c8ed13f3c7acbd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.43.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.43.33" sID="gen5415" type="section"/> <div sID="gen5416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33. </hi><hi type="italic">The first-born according to his birthright</hi> <note n="170"> <div sID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> “It appears that the brothers of Joseph sat before him at the table, while, according to patriarchal practice, they were accustomed to recline. It appears from the sculptures, that the Egyptians also were in the habit of sitting at table, although they had couches.” — Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 39. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> </note> Although of the sons of Jacob four were born of bond-women; yet, since they were the elder, they had precedence of their younger brethren, who had descended from free-born mothers; whence it appears that they had been accustomed by their father to keep this order. What, then, some one may say, becomes of the declaration, “the son of the bond-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free-woman?” Truly, I think, since Ishmael was rejected, by the divine oracle proceeding from the mouth of Sarah, as Esau was afterwards, Jacob was fully taught that he had as many heirs as he had sons. Hence arose that equality which caused each to keep his place, first, middle, or last, according to his age. But the design of Moses was to show, that although Benjamin was the youngest, yet he was preferred to all the rest in honor; because Joseph could not refrain from giving him the principal token of his love. It was, indeed, his intention to remain unknown; but affection so far prevails, that, beyond the purpose of his mind, he suddenly breaks out into a declaration of his affection. From the concluding portion of the chapter we gather, what I recently intimated, that the feast was unusually luxurious, and that they were received to it, in a liberal and joyful manner, beyond the daily custom. For the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שכר</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shakar</hi>,) they “were merry,” signifies, either that they were not always accustomed to drink wine, or that there was more than ordinary indulgence at the sumptuous tables spread for them. Here, however, no intemperance is implied, (so that drunkards may not plead the example of the holy fathers as a pretext for their crime,) but an honorable and moderate liberality. I acknowledge, indeed, that the word has a double meaning, and is often taken in an ill sense; as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.21">Genesis 9:21</reference>, and in similar places: but in the present instance the design of Moses is clear. Should any one object, that a frugal use of food and drink is simply that which suffices for the nourishing of the body: I answer, although food is properly for the supply of our necessities, yet the legitimate use of it may proceed further. For it is not in vain, that our food has savor as well as vital nutriment; but thus our heavenly Father sweetly delights us with his delicacies. And his benignity is not in vain commended in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.15">Psalm 104:15</reference>, where he is said to create “wine that maketh glad the heart of man.” Nevertheless, the more kindly he indulges us, the more solicitously ought we to restrict ourselves to a frugal use of his gifts. For we know how unbridled are the appetites of the flesh. Whence it happens that, in abundance, it is almost always lascivious, and in penury, impatient. We must, however, adhere to St. Paul’s method, that we know how to abound and to suffer need; that is, we must take great care if we have unusual plenty, that it does not hurry us into luxury; and, on the other hand, we must see to it, that we bear poverty with an equal mind. Some one, perhaps, will say, that the flesh is more than sufficiently ingenious in giving a specious color to its excesses; and, therefore, nothing more should be allowed to it than necessity demands. And, truly, I confess, we must diligently attend to what Paul prescribes, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.13.14">Romans 13:14</reference>,)<div eID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5418" type="x-p"/>“Make not provision for the flesh to fulfill the lusts thereof.”<div eID="gen5418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5419" type="x-p"/>But because it greatly concerns all pious people to receive their food from the hand of God, with quiet consciences, it is necessary for them to know to what extent the use of food and wine is lawful.<div eID="gen5419" type="x-p"/><div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.43.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen5415" osisID="Gen.43.33" type="section"/><div eID="gen5324"/><div eID="gen5322"/> <div sID="gen5420"/> <div sID="gen5421" type="x-p"/>CHAPTER 44.<div eID="gen5421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5422"/> <table> <row> <cell> <div sID="gen5423" type="x-p"/><reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.1-Gen.44.34">Genesis 44:1-34</reference><div eID="gen5423" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi>And he commanded the steward of his house, saying, Fill the men’s sacks <hi type="italic">with</hi> food, as much as they can carry, and put every man’s money in his sack’s mouth.<div eID="gen5424" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen5425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi>Et praecepit praefecto domus suae, dicendo, Imple saccos virorum esca, quantum potuerint ferre, et pone pecuniam uniuscujusque in ore sacci sui,<div eID="gen5425" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen5426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2. </hi>And put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack’s mouth of the youngest, and his corn money. Ne forte videam malum quod inveniet patrem meum.<div eID="gen5491" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row> </table> <div sID="gen5492" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5492" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="43" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XLIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND the famine was sore in the land.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And it came to pass when they had eaten up the corn which they had brought out of Egypt, their father said unto them, Go again, buy us a little food <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He saith, <ns0:hi>a little,</ns0:hi> either to shew, that he took no thought to satisfie his or their curiosity or luxury, but onely their ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity, for which a little would suffice, and that they must all moderate their appetites, especially in a time of such scarci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty: or to encourage them to the journey by suggesting to them that they needed not bring great stores but onely what was sufficient for that year, and that God would provide bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter for them hereafter so as they should not need to go so far for corn any more.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And Judah spake unto him, saying, The man did <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> protesting he protested.</ns0:note> solemnly protest unto us saying, Ye shall not see my face <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">See the same expression 2 <ns0:hi>S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>m.</ns0:hi> 14. 24, 32. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20. 25, 38. Ye shall not be admitted into my presence, nor to the purchasing of any corn here.</ns0:note> except your <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 42. 20. and 44. 23.</ns0:note> brother be with you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 If thou wilt send our brother with us, we will go down and buy thee food.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 But if thou wilt not send <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> we will not go down <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Because we shall both lose the end of our journey, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the getting of corn, and run the utmost hazard of all our lives.</ns0:note>, for the man said unto us, Ye shall not see my face, except your brother <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And Israel said, Wherefore dealt ye so ill with me, as to tell the man whether ye had yet a brother?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And they said, The man <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> asking he asked us.</ns0:note> asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred, saying, Is your father yet alive? have ye another brother? and we told him according to the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> mouth.</ns0:note> tenour of these words <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">We gave answers su<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ble to his questions, or such as his words required.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> knowing could we know.</ns0:note> could we certainly know that he would say, Bring your brother down?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And Judah <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Who for his age and prudence and penitent carriage for his youthful follies was most beloved and regarded by his father.</ns0:note> said unto Israel his father, Send the lad <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">So he calls him, because he was the youngest of all, though he was now 30 years old, and a father of divers children. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 22. and 35. 18. and 41. 46. and 46. 21.</ns0:note> with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live, and not die, both we and thou, and also our little ones.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 I will be surety for him: of my hand shalt thou require him: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 44. 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> If I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>be an offender to thee,</ns0:hi> Let me bear the guilt and shame and punishment due to so great an offence.</ns0:note> for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 For except we had lingered, surely now we had returned <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> twice by this.</ns0:note> this second time.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And their father Israel said unto them, If it must <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> so now, do this: take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney, spices, and myrrhe <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Of all which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 37. 25.</ns0:note>, nuts <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That kind of nuts which we call <ns0:hi>pistaches,</ns0:hi> as some Hebrew and other expositours render the word; for that was both an excellent fruit and peculiar to <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> and well agreeing with the <ns0:hi>almonds</ns0:hi> which here follow.</ns0:note> and al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monds.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And take double money <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Double to what you carried last, either to procure more corn, which may prevent the frequency of such perillous jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nies: or because the continuance and increase of the scarcity had advanced the price.</ns0:note> in your hand, and the money that was brought again in the mouth of your sacks: carry <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> again <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For it is their money, not ours, and therefore must be restored.</ns0:note> in your hand, peradventure it was an oversight <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either in you, or in the receiver of your money, who through multitude of buyers and haste in his business might easily be mistaken.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Take also your brother, and arise, go a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gain unto the man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may send away your other bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, and Benjamin: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>and I, as I have been,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">An expression whereby he submits himself and children to Gods will and providence, whatever the issue shall be. Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 4. 16. Or thus, <ns0:hi>As I have been</ns0:hi> already <ns0:hi>bereaved</ns0:hi> of some of my dearest children, so <ns0:hi>I shall be bereaved</ns0:hi> of the rest, and I shall be left solitary, and if this be my portion, Gods will be done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the men took that present, and they took double money in their hand, and Benjamin, and rose up, and went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And when Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the ruler of his house, Bring these men home, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> killing.</ns0:note> slay, and make ready: for these men shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> dine with me at noon <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The usual time for the more solemn meal in the East Countries, as the evening was the time, and the supper the great meal among the <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:41" />17 And the man did as Joseph bade: and the man brought the men into Josephs house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And the men were afraid, because they were brought into Josephs house, and they said, Because of the money that was returned in our sacks at the first time, are we brought in, that he may <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> roll him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self upon us.</ns0:note> seek occasion against us, and fall upon us, and take us for bondmen <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The proper punishment for thieves.</ns0:note>, and our asses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And they came near to the Steward of Jo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sephs house, and they communed with him at the door of the house;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And said, O Sir, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 42. 3.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> coming <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, we came <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> we came indeed down at the first time to buy food.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 42. 27.</ns0:note> it came to pass when we came to the Inne, that we opened our sacks, and behold, every mans money <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight: and we have brought it again in our hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And other money have we brought down in our hands to buy food: we cannot tell who put our money in our sacks.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And he said, Peace <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> to you <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">No harm shall come to you for that matter.</ns0:note>, fear not: your God, and the God of your father <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Thus he speaks, because <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> had instructed him, as well as others of his family, in the true Religion.</ns0:note> hath given you treasure in your sacks <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By his power and provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence secretly putting it there.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> your mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney came to me.</ns0:note> I had your money. And he brought Simeon out unto them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the man brought the men into Josephs house, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 18. 4. and 24. 32.</ns0:note> gave <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> water, and they washed their feet, and he gave their asses provender.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And they made ready the present against Joseph came at noon: for they heard that they should eat bread there.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And when Joseph came home, they brought him the present which was in their hand, into the house, and bowed themselves to him to the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And he asked them of their <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> peace.</ns0:note> welfare, and said, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. is there <ns0:hi>peace to your fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Is your father well, the old man <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 42. 11, 13.</ns0:note> of whom ye spake? Is he yet alive?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And they answered, Thy servant <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By which expression delivered in <ns0:hi>Iacobs</ns0:hi> name and by his order <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> himself <ns0:hi>made obeisance to him,</ns0:hi> as was foretold, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 37. 9.</ns0:note> our father <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in good health, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> yet alive: and they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And he lift up his eyes, and saw <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) More narrowly observed him, having now more leasure, than he seems to have had when he saw him first, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 16.</ns0:note> his bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Benjamin, his mothers son, and said, Is this your younger brother, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 42. 13.</ns0:note> of whom ye spake unto me? and he said, God be gracious unto thee my son <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">So he calls him, not from special affection, which he in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended not yet to discover; but because this compellation is commonly used when a man speaks to another who is his inferi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our in age, or dignity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And Joseph made haste: for his bowels did yern <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">His heart and inward parts were vehemently moved, as they commonly are upon occasion of any excessive passion, of love, pity, grief, or joy, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> upon his brother: and he sought where to weep, and he entred into his chamber, and wept there.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And he washed his face, and went out, and refrained himself, and said, Set on bread.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And they set on for him by himself <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Partly because the dignity of his place and the custom of Princes required this state: and partly for the reason here following.</ns0:note>, and for them by themselves, and for the Egyptians which did eat with him, by themselves: because the Egyptians might not eat bread with the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brews, for that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> an abomination unto the E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gyptians <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Not so much from their pride and disdain of other people, as from their superstition and idolatry: partly because they worshipped the creatures, which the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> and others did commonly eat: and partly because of some peculiar rites and customes which they had in the dressing and ordering of their diet. Whence <ns0:hi>Herodotus</ns0:hi> affirms, that the <ns0:hi>Egyptians</ns0:hi> would not use the pots nor knives of the <ns0:hi>Graecians</ns0:hi> about their food. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 46. 34. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 8. 26.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And they sate before him, the first-born according to his birth-right, and the youngest according to his youth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Being so placed either by <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> appointment: or rather by their own choice and according to their custome; by which the elder, though the handmaidens children, took place of the younger, who by that order were taught what veneration they owe to the aged, and how great a sin it is, though very custo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mary, in young men to despise those whom they should reve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence.</ns0:note>: and the men <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not the <ns0:hi>Egyptians,</ns0:hi> but the <ns0:hi>Hebrews,</ns0:hi> the men last spoken of.</ns0:note> marvel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either at the matter and manner of the feasts and entertainments of the <ns0:hi>Egyptians;</ns0:hi> or rather at the singular honour which <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> did to them above all others, the reason whereof they could not conceive, and therefore marvelled at it.</ns0:note> one at another.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And he took, and <ns0:hi>sent</ns0:hi> messes unto them from before him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It was the antient custom of <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> and other countries, in their feasts, that either all the meat, or at least some eminent parts and parcels of it, were not promiscuously set before all the guests, but peculiarly distributed by the master of the feast to the several guests, and that differently according to his respect and affection to them, or to their several qualities. See 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 5. and 9. 22, 23, 24.</ns0:note>: but Benjamins mess <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> five times so much as any of theirs <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Partly because of his near<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er relation and dearer affection to him, and partly to observe whether this would raise that envy in them towards him, which was the occasion of their malicious enterprize against himself, that he might accordingly provide for his security.</ns0:note>: and they drunk, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> they drank largely.</ns0:note> were merry <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew</ns0:hi> word oft signifies to <ns0:hi>be drunk,</ns0:hi> but oft-times it is onely to <ns0:hi>drink liberally,</ns0:hi> though not to drunkenness, as may appear from <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 5. 1. <ns0:hi>Hag.</ns0:hi> 1. 6. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2. 10.</ns0:note> with him.</ns0:p>
